statement: A single op amp with R1/R2 on the inverting path and an R3/R4 divider on the noninverting input acts as a difference amplifier with vO = (R2/R1)(vI2 - vI1) provided R4/R3 = R2/R1 (usually implemented as R3 = R1, R4 = R2). Differential input resistance is Rid = 2R1.
required_blocks: R1 from vI1 to inverting input
R2 feedback from output to inverting input
R3 from vI2 to noninverting input
R4 from noninverting input to ground, with R4/R3 = R2/R1
design_notes: Design example (Sedra Ex. D2.16): input resistance 20 kohm and gain 10 -> R1 = R3 = 10 kohm, R2 = R4 = 100 kohm.
Drawback: large differential gain forces R1 small, so Rid = 2R1 becomes low; gain cannot be varied without changing two resistor ratios simultaneously.
Resistor-ratio matching sets CMRR; use the instrumentation amplifier when high input resistance or adjustable gain is required.
condition: Fixed-gain subtraction of two signals when source impedances are low compared with R1/R3 and the required gain is known at design time.

statement: If the resistor ratios of a single-op-amp difference amplifier are mismatched (R4/R3 != R2/R1), the common-mode gain Acm = (R4/(R4+R3))(1 - (R2/R1)(R3/R4)) becomes nonzero and CMRR is finite, so common-mode input appears at the output. With 1%-tolerance resistors in a gain-100 design (R1 = R3 = 2 kohm, R2 = R4 = 200 kohm), worst-case Acm = 0.04 V/V and CMRR drops to 68 dB.
condition: Any single-op-amp difference amplifier built from discrete tolerance-limited resistors, especially with large common-mode input (e.g., shunt sensing or transducer lines carrying interference).
consequence: Common-mode voltage leaks to the output as error; a 1% resistor set limits worst-case CMRR to 68 dB at Ad = 100 (40 dB).

statement: The three-op-amp instrumentation amplifier uses two noninverting input buffers sharing one floating gain resistor 2R1 (each with feedback R2), followed by a unity- or fixed-gain difference amplifier (R3, R4). Overall differential gain is Ad = (R4/R3)(1 + R2/R1), input resistance is ideally infinite at both inputs, and gain is set by the single resistor 2R1.
inputs: vI1, vI2: small differential signal possibly riding on a large common-mode voltage
required_blocks: 2x op amps A1, A2 as first-stage buffers with gain, sharing floating resistor 2R1 between their inverting inputs
1x op amp A3 with R3/R3/R4/R4 as second-stage difference amplifier
Optional: 2R1 = fixed R1f in series with pot R1v for adjustable gain
design_notes: First stage amplifies the differential signal by (1 + R2/R1) while passing common mode at unity gain (no current flows in 2R1 for common-mode input), easing the CMRR burden on the second stage.
Put the bulk of the gain in the first stage; design the second stage for gain 1 (R4 = R3).
Proper operation does not require the two R2 resistors to match (mismatch only slightly alters Ad, Eq. 2.23).
Integrated single-package instrumentation amplifiers implementing this topology are widely available; prefer them for portable/medical-grade precision front ends.
condition: Amplifying small differential signals (e.g., 1-mV transducer output) in the presence of large common-mode interference (e.g., 1 V on the leads), when high input resistance and single-resistor gain adjustment are required.

statement: If the node between the two first-stage gain resistors of a three-op-amp instrumentation amplifier is grounded (Fig. 2.20a variant) instead of left floating, the input common-mode voltage is amplified by the same factor (1 + R2/R1) as the differential signal; the first-stage outputs can then saturate the op amps, and even without saturation the second stage must reject much larger common-mode signals, so overall CMRR is inevitably reduced. The grounded variant also requires perfectly matched first-stage channels and two simultaneously varied resistors to change gain.
condition: Three-op-amp in-amp first stage with the shared gain-resistor midpoint tied to ground, operated with nonzero common-mode input.
consequence: Op-amp saturation at the first-stage outputs and/or degraded overall CMRR; remedy is the standard wiring with one floating 2R1 resistor.

statement: Choose between the single-op-amp difference amplifier and the three-op-amp instrumentation amplifier based on source impedance, required gain adjustability, and common-mode magnitude relative to the differential signal.
conditions: Use the single-op-amp difference amplifier for fixed gain with low source impedance (its Rid = 2R1 loads the source).
Use the instrumentation amplifier when the source impedance is high or unequal, since its buffered inputs give ideally infinite input resistance at both terminals.
Use the instrumentation amplifier when gain must be adjustable: one external resistor (2R1, or RG in Sadiku's Av = 1 + 2R/RG form) sets gain without disturbing matching.
Use the instrumentation amplifier for small differential signals on large common-mode interference, e.g., a 1-mV transducer signal with about 1 V of interference on each lead (Sedra 2.4 example).
tradeoffs: Difference amp: 1 op amp and 4 resistors, but Rid = 2R1 shrinks as gain (R2/R1) rises, and varying gain requires changing two matched ratios simultaneously.
In-amp: 3 op amps and 7 resistors, but first stage amplifies only the differential signal (common mode passes at unity), improving effective CMRR of the chain.
In-amp gain formula Ad = (R4/R3)(1 + R2/R1); commercial single-package IAs (e.g., LH0036 cited by Sadiku) span gain 1 to 1000 with RG from 100 ohm to 10 kohm.
failure_modes: Either topology: resistor-ratio mismatch makes Acm nonzero and CMRR finite (1% resistors -> worst-case 68 dB at gain 100).
In-amp with grounded gain-resistor midpoint: common mode amplified -> op-amp saturation, reduced CMRR.
Difference amp at high gain: low input resistance loads high-impedance sources and degrades accuracy.
condition: Selecting the differential front-end topology for sensor, bridge, or shunt-voltage measurement in a larger design.

source.book: Sedra/Smith Microelectronic Circuits 7e (with Sadiku FEC 7e Sec. 5.10.2 gain form)

statement: Sedra Example 2.3 designs a three-op-amp instrumentation amplifier whose gain is adjustable from 2 to 1000 using a 100-kohm potentiometer as part of the first-stage gain resistor.
problem: Design the in-amp of Fig. 2.20(b) for a gain variable over 2 to 1000 using a 100-kohm pot.
assumptions: All required gain is placed in the first stage; second stage set to gain 1.
All second-stage resistors set to a convenient equal value of 10 kohm.
steps: Implement 2R1 as fixed R1f in series with pot resistance R1v (0 to 100 kohm).
Impose 1 + 2R2/(R1f + 100 kohm) = 2 (minimum gain at pot = 100 kohm).
Solve simultaneously: R1f = 100.2 ohm, R2 = 50.050 kohm.
result: Exact values R1f = 100.2 ohm and R2 = 50.050 kohm; practical standard 1%-tolerance metal-film choices R1f = 100 ohm and R2 = 49.9 kohm cover approximately the required 2-1000 gain range; second-stage resistors all 10 kohm.
condition: Wide-range single-knob gain adjustment in an in-amp; R1f is mandatory in series with the pot to limit maximum gain (pot at zero must not short the gain resistor).

statement: A comparator with hysteresis (Schmitt trigger) is an op amp in a positive-feedback loop with divider R1/R2; regenerative switching between saturation levels L+ and L- gives two thresholds. Inverting form (input at op-amp inverting input): VTH = beta*L+ and VTL = beta*L- with beta = R1/(R1+R2). Noninverting form (input through R1 to the noninverting node): VTL = -L+(R1/R2), VTH = -L-(R1/R2).
inputs: vI: possibly noisy analog signal to be compared against threshold(s)
outputs: vO: two-level output at L+ or L- (op-amp saturation levels), switching with hysteresis width VTH - VTL
required_blocks: 1x op amp (or comparator) driven open-loop into saturation levels L+ / L-
R1 from output-divider node to ground (inverting form) or from input (noninverting form)
R2 from output to the noninverting input node
Positive-feedback loop gain A*beta > 1 (normally guaranteed by large open-loop A)
design_notes: Size the hysteresis width to exceed the expected peak-to-peak interference amplitude on the input; VTH and VTL are usually separated by a small amount, e.g., 100 mV (Sedra Fig. 18.23-18.24).
Verified sizing example (Exercise 18.18, noninverting circuit): L+ = -L- = 10 V, R1 = 1 kohm -> R2 = 200 kohm gives 100-mV hysteresis width.
Output levels can be made precise by clamping with zener/diode limiter networks instead of relying on op-amp saturation (Fig. 18.25).
The same bistable in a feedback loop with an RC circuit forms an astable square-wave generator (Sec. 18.5).
condition: Threshold detection, zero-crossing detection, waveform squaring, or ADC front-end comparison on signals carrying noise/interference; positive feedback (not negative) is mandatory.

statement: A single-threshold comparator processing a signal with superimposed higher-frequency interference crosses the threshold multiple times around each intended crossing, so the output changes state several times per event; in a zero-crossing counter this directly corrupts the count. The fix is to add hysteresis whose width (VTH - VTL, e.g., about 100 mV) exceeds the expected peak-to-peak interference amplitude, so the output switches exactly once per genuine crossing.
condition: Comparator input slews slowly through the threshold while carrying noise/interference of known peak-to-peak amplitude (common for sensor and mains-derived signals).
consequence: Output chatter: multiple spurious transitions per crossing, false event counts, potential downstream logic glitches.

values.typical_hysteresis_separation: 100 mV (Sedra: 'usually VTH and VTL are separated by a small amount, say 100 mV')

statement: Sedra's recommended analog-to-digital acquisition chain: a high-input-impedance, high-gain, high-CMRR differential amplifier directly at the transducer output, followed by a filter to eliminate interference, then a sample-and-hold, then the ADC. The S/H itself is an analog switch (implementable as a MOSFET transmission gate) that closes for a short time tau out of each clock period T, a storage capacitor that holds the sample, and a buffer amplifier driving the ADC input.
inputs: Analog transducer/sensor signal, possibly differential with common-mode interference
outputs: Held sample voltage per clock period, fed to the A/D converter; N-bit code from the ADC
required_blocks: Differential/instrumentation amplifier (high input impedance, high CMRR) at the transducer
Interference-elimination filter between amplifier and sampler
Analog switch (MOSFET transmission gate), clock-controlled, closure time tau << period T
Buffer amplifier between hold capacitor and ADC
design_notes: The buffer prevents the ADC input from discharging the hold capacitor; the switch must be closed only a small fraction tau of each period T.
Quantization: an N-bit code represents 2^N levels (4 bits -> 16 values); using more bits reduces quantization error but requires more complex circuitry.
Neither Sadiku nor Sedra gives numeric guidance for sizing an external ADC input RC filter (settling vs droop); do not cite these books for such values.
condition: Digitizing an analog sensor signal for digital processing; sampling justified by the sampling (Shannon) theorem.

source.book: Sedra/Smith Microelectronic Circuits (legacy Ch. 9 data-converter section bundled in this PDF)

statement: To extend a current meter (movement full-scale current Im, internal resistance Rm) to measure full-scale current Ifs, connect a shunt resistor Rn in parallel with the movement sized by Rn = Im*Rm/(Ifs - Im); the shunt (and meter) resistance is deliberately made very small, theoretically zero, to minimize the voltage drop inserted into the measured branch. Verified example (Sadiku Practice Prob. 2.17): Im = 1 mA, Rm = 50 ohm gives Rn = 50 milliohm for 0-1 A, 505 milliohm for 0-100 mA, and 5.556 ohm for 0-10 mA ranges.
condition: Series (in-line) current measurement with a parallel shunt; the sensing element must be low-resistance so the inserted voltage drop (burden) does not disturb the measured circuit. The small shunt voltage is what a difference/instrumentation amplifier front end would amplify.
design_notes: Failure mode: a too-large shunt/meter resistance drops significant voltage across the sensing element and changes the branch current being measured.
Multi-range designs switch between several shunt values (Fig. 2.61b).

statement: For the standard packaged three-op-amp instrumentation amplifier with all internal resistors equal to R and one external gain-set resistor RG between the gain-set pins, the output is vo = Av(v2 - v1) with Av = 1 + 2R/RG. Verified example (Sadiku Ex. 5.13): R = 10 kohm, RG = 500 ohm -> Av = 41; inputs 2.011 V and 2.017 V (6-mV difference on ~2-V common mode) -> vo = 246 mV.
condition: Using a single-package IA (Sadiku cites the LH0036: gain adjustable 1 to 1000 with external RG from 100 ohm to 10 kohm) for low-level signals in process control, thermocouple amplification, or data acquisition.

values.example: R=10 kohm, RG=500 ohm -> Av=41, 6 mV in -> 246 mV out

design_notes: Gain is set by the single external resistor RG; input impedance of both inputs is very high and does not vary with gain; output depends only on the input difference (common-mode voltages cancel).
Companion sizing example (Practice Prob. 5.13): gain 142 with R = 25 kohm requires RG = 354.6 ohm.
